description:
We are Double Western Bacon, a team of students passionate about software development, technology, science, and creative problem-solving. Our skills include programming, software engineering, and digital design. We enjoy building practical tools, interactive experiences, and polished interfaces. For this challenge, we aim to combine scientific data and technology to explore planetary environments and support future space exploration.

IBT & IMT @ Tec de Monterrey (Itesm).
summary: MVJ (Mars Viability Journey) is a desktop application that helps decide where on Earth to test a Mars mission. The user picks a mission (rover, landing, mining or a Martian base) and sets its limits and priorities. MVJ ranks the best regions on Mars for that mission, then searches the entire Earth for comparable places to test it, using 15 open datasets including NASA MOLA, TES, EMIT, MODIS and MERRA-2. Every result explains what is similar, what is not, and how much of the score is backed by real data. The result can be explored in a 3D scene with real terrain, and an AI agent, Alien Brother, lets anyone operate the tool in plain language while the scores come only from a transparent, validated algorithm. This matters because terrestrial analogs are usually chosen from fixed catalogs or by visual resemblance, with no shared criteria. MVJ turns that choice into an explainable, mission-specific comparison, so students, university teams and outreach programs can ask the right question: similar in what, for which mission, and with what evidence?
details:
MVJ (Mars Viability Journey) answers a concrete question: if we had to test a Mars mission tomorrow, where on Earth should we test it, and how similar would that place really be?

What it does and how it works:

The user picks a mission (rover deployment, landing, mining prospection or a Martian base) and sets its hard limits and priorities. MVJ divides Mars and Earth into an icosphere of equal-area cells (about 400 km² each, 327,680 on Mars and 1.3 million on Earth) and fills them with layers from 15 open datasets, including NASA MOLA, TES, Mars Odyssey GRS, EMIT, MODIS, MERRA-2, SRTM15+, SWIM and WorldClim. First, every Mars cell passes, fails or stays unknown for each limit; missing data is never invented. Then each variable is scored by how close it is to the mission's target and weighted by the user's priorities, with a coverage percentage that shows how much of the score is backed by real data.

Regions grow cell by cell and stop where the terrain changes. The user picks a Mars destination, and MVJ searches the entire Earth for comparable regions, explaining what is similar, what is not, and which analogs are already known. It also works in reverse: from a place on Earth, such as Lake Titicaca, to candidate regions on Mars. Finally, the result can be explored in a 3D scene with real relief. Alien Brother, an AI agent, lets anyone operate the tool in plain language, but every score comes from the algorithm, never from the AI.

Benefits and intended impact:

Terrestrial analogs are usually chosen from fixed expert catalogs or by visual resemblance, with no shared criteria. MVJ makes the choice explicit, mission-specific and explainable. It is intended as a tool for exploration, learning and regional pre-selection for students, teachers, university space and robotics teams, and museums and outreach programs.

Tools and technologies:

The application is written in C# with .NET 10 and Raylib (3D rendering, custom shaders, synthesized music and sound effects). The data pipeline uses more than 20 Python scripts with numpy to download, convert and validate each dataset. Alien Brother uses an OpenAI-compatible language model. The interface is available in English and Spanish.

Creativity:

MVJ starts from the mission instead of the place. It searches the whole planet instead of a fixed list, compares measured physical data instead of images, works in both directions, and shows the limits of every analogy alongside its similarity. We chose a deterministic, transparent algorithm over machine learning because there are only about 29 known analogs to learn from, and a trained model would just repeat them. We wanted to find new analogs and be able to explain every number.

Factors we considered:

Scientific honesty was central. The score is a similarity, not a probability of success. Missing data lowers coverage instead of being filled in. Earth cannot reproduce Mars' gravity, thin atmosphere or radiation, and the app says so. We validated the work before trusting it: 69 algorithm tests and 150 independent data tests all pass. For Jezero and Gale, known analogs rank in the 96th percentile against 83–85 for random points, and for flat plains such as Oxia Planum, where they show no advantage, we report it openly.
